title: The elephant in the dark
hookLine: people feel an elephant in a dark room, and each describes a different thing (Masnavi 3)

lines: AN ELEPHANT IN A DARK HOUSE.
THEY REACH OUT WITH THEIR HANDS.
cards: Two people describe the same event, the same boss, the same family dinner, and it sounds like two different places. Each one is completely sure. Each one is partly right.

And nobody's listening. In the third book of the Masnavi, Rumi tells a short story. Some people from India bring an elephant to a town where nobody has ever seen one, and they keep it in a dark house.
Curious, people file in, one by one, to find out what an elephant is. It's too dark to see anything. So they reach out with their hands.

teach.h: A PIPE, A FAN, A PILLAR, A THRONE.
teach.b: One man's hand lands on the trunk, and he comes out saying: an elephant is like a water pipe. Another touches an ear: no, it's like a fan. Another feels a leg: it's a pillar.
Another runs his palm along its back: it's like a throne.
Each is describing something real. Each is wrong about the elephant. Then Rumi adds the line the story turns on: if each of them had held a candle, their differences would have gone away.
Rumi didn't invent the story. An older Persian poet, Sana'i, told a version, and a version was told in India centuries before either of them. It traveled far.
But notice what Rumi does with it.

teach.h: THE PALM CAN'T HOLD THE WHOLE.
teach.b: The eye of the senses, he says, is like the palm of a hand: the palm can't hold the whole of the elephant. The people aren't stupid, or lying. They're in the dark, trusting a hand to do the work of a light.

teach.h: THE CANDLE IS A LIGHT FROM GOD.
teach.b: For Rumi, the candle is the light that comes from God, the light of an inner sight that sees the whole. Readers have used the story in many ways since.
At the very least, it asks for some humility: the thing you're touching is real, and it's probably not the whole elephant.

how: The elephant in the dark is a story from the Masnavi taught in Sufi circles and schools as a lesson in the limits of the senses and the need for the inner light that comes from God.

o: a candle, the light that shows the whole
the palm of the hand that feels in the dark
a shadow that hides what's really there

games.q: what each one touched — tap the pairs.

s: Rumi invented the story of the elephant
Sana'i told a version before him, and a version was told in India centuries earlier.
in Rumi's telling, the people are lying
each describes something real; they're in the dark, trusting a hand to do the work of a light.
Rumi says a candle would have ended their differences
if each had held a candle, their differences would have gone away.

games.q: four people come out of the dark house with four different descriptions of the elephant. what does Rumi say would fix it?
games.why: a candle: if each had held one, their differences would have gone away. for Rumi, the light of inner sight from God.

practice: Think of someone you disagree with, about something small or something big, and picture them in the dark room, describing the part of the elephant under their hand. What's real in what they're saying?
Imagine listening to the end without preparing your answer, and if you pray, ask for light, for both of you.

wordCard.voice: Sham'. A candle — the light that, Rumi says, would have let each one touching the elephant in the dark see the whole. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic and Persian: a candle, the light that would have shown the whole elephant.

carryVoice: Your line: a candle would help. Every hand is on something real. That's day three hundred.
